items.label: text
items.text: When we do this experiment in practice, it is not very often that the ratio comes out as 1:1. There are things that may go wrong with this experiment which could affect the results, such as:

items.label: list_item
items.text: some of the magnesium oxide powder might escape when the lid is lifted

items.label: list_item
items.text: not all the magnesium might have reacted

items.label: list_item
items.text: the magnesium can also react with nitrogen in the air.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: The original masses were measured to 2 significant figures so the number of moles should also be given to 2 significant figures (0.010). If you write 0.01 for the number of moles of atoms in the exam, this will be fine and still give you the correct answer.

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: The teacher demonstrating needs to wear a face shield and use safety screens. The pupils require eye protection and should be no closer than 2 metres. If a drying agent is needed anhydrous calcium chloride should be used NOT concentrated sulfuric acid.

items.label: section_header
items.text: KEYPOINT

items.label: text
items.text: We must always make sure that the tube is filled with hydrogen before lighting the stream of hydrogen because a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen is explosive! It is therefore important to let the stream of hydrogen gas flow through the tube for a little while (to flush out all the oxygen) before lighting it or lighting the Bunsen burner.

items.label: text
items.text: In order to find the formula of magnesium oxide we need to work out how many moles of magnesium atoms combine with how many moles of oxygen atoms.

items.label: table
items.text:
|                                                                              | Mg          | 0           |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------|-------------|
| masses/g                                                                     | 0.24        | 0.16        |
| find the number of moles of atoms by dividing the mass by the mass of 1 mole | 0.24/24     | 0.16/16     |
| number of moles of atoms                                                     | 0.010       | 0.010       |
| divide by the smaller number to find the ratio                               | 0.010/0.010 | 0.010/0.010 |
| ratio of moles                                                               | 1           | 1           |
| empirical formula                                                            | Mg0         | Mg0         |

items.label: text
items.text: The empirical formula of magnesium oxide is MgO.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE FORMULA FOR COPPER OXIDE

items.label: section_header
items.text: ACTIVITY 4

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: INVESTIGATING THE FORMULA OF A METAL OXIDE BY REDUCTION

items.label: text
items.text: We can also find the formula of an oxide by removing the oxygen from it and looking at how the mass changes.

items.label: text
items.text: The following procedure can be used to find the formula of copper oxide:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Weigh a ceramic dish.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Put about 3g of copper oxide in the ceramic dish and weigh the dish again.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Place the ceramic dish in a tube as shown in Figure 5.13.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Pass hydrogen gas over the copper oxide.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Ignite the excess hydrogen, which comes out of the small hole in the boiling tube.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Heat the copper oxide strongly until the reaction is finished (pinkbrown copper metal will be seen).
